text: Klinefelter syndrome (KS), also known as 47,XXY, is a chromosomal condition in which a male has an extra X chromosome, resulting in a total of 47 or more chromosomes instead of the usual 46. It is named after American endocrinologist Harry Klinefelter, who first described the condition in 1942 with colleagues Fuller Albright and E. C. Reifenstein at Massachusetts General Hospital, and it was later confirmed in 1956 to result from an extra chromosome. The syndrome is diagnosed through karyotyping, which analyzes chromosomes in blood cells, and may also involve testing of oral mucosa cells to detect mosaicism. The birth prevalence of KS in Victoria, Australia is estimated at 223 per 100,000 males, and the overall prevalence in the general male population is approximately four per 10,000 (0.04%). KS occurs randomly due to nondisjunction during gametogenesis—either in paternal meiosis I, maternal meiosis I, or maternal meiosis II—where sex chromosomes fail to separate, leading to an XXY karyotype. The extra X chromosome is inherited from the mother in about 50% of cases, and maternal age is the only known risk factor, with women aged 40 having a four-times higher risk than those aged 24. In XXY males, most genes on the extra X chromosome are inactivated, except for those in pseudoautosomal regions that can be expressed. Symptoms often appear at puberty and include infertility, small testicles (typically less than 2 cm in length and 1 cm in width, with a volume of 4 ml or less), reduced muscle mass, less body and facial hair, broader hips, poor motor coordination, gynecomastia (breast growth), and low libido. Gynecomastia occurs in up to 80% of cases, with about 10% seeking surgical removal. Approximately 50% of males with KS can produce sperm, and advanced reproductive techniques like intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) with testicular sperm extraction (TESE) have enabled biological offspring in over 100 reported cases by 2010. Mosaic forms, such as 47,XXY/46,XY, occur in about 15–20% of cases and are associated with milder symptoms, including normal male secondary sex characteristics. Variants like 48,XXYY or 48,XXXY occur in one in 18,000–50,000 male births, and 49,XXXXY in one in 85,000 to 100,000 male births. Individuals with KS are at increased risk for autoimmune disorders, breast cancer, venous thromboembolic disease, osteoporosis, and cardiovascular disease due to metabolic issues like dyslipidemia and type 2 diabetes, though hypertension is not linked to the condition. The syndrome is associated with language delays, reading difficulties, executive function deficits, and a 10% autism prevalence, with 25% to 85% experiencing some language problem. Behavioral issues such as anxiety, depression, mood dysregulation, and poor social skills are common, and children may be quiet, shy, and less active. Despite these challenges, adults with KS often lead normal lives with friends and families, though some face social and emotional difficulties. The lifespan is reduced by about 2.1 years compared to the general male population. Hypogonadism in KS refers to decreased hormone production, not just small testicles, and is characterized by low testosterone, high follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) levels, leading to impaired spermatogenesis. Testicular dysfunction results from destruction of seminiferous tubules and reduced function of Sertoli and Leydig cells. Diagnosis is often prompted by symptoms such as small testes, infertility, gynecomastia, tall stature, long limbs, developmental delay, or learning issues. KS has been identified in ancient burials, including a 1000 AD man in Portugal and a person buried with the Suontaka sword, whose gender identity may have been non-binary. Historically, symptoms like infertility and gynecomastia led to social stigma due to perceived lack of masculinity, but awareness and advocacy have reduced stigma. The classification of KS as an intersex variation is debated; some intersex groups and academics include it, while traditional medical views have excluded it, often prioritizing physical appearance. A 2024 study found that 19% of KS respondents identified as intersex or non-binary, 12% as female, and 53% as male, with 56% noting a discrepancy between gender identity and physical appearance. Only about 25% of individuals with KS are diagnosed in their lifetime, and the syndrome is the main cause of male hypogonadism. The rate among infertile males is 3.1%, and it is more common in transgender women than in the general population.
